strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem in massively parallel continuous-control RL: obtaining low-variance pathwise policy updates without the memory and stability costs of large off-policy replay buffers.

The proposed REPPO algorithm is a coherent combination of on-policy TD-lambda Q learning, entropy regularization, KL-constrained policy updates, categorical value learning, normalization, and an auxiliary prediction loss.

Empirical evaluation is broad, covering 23 MuJoCo Playground DMC tasks and 8 ManiSkill tasks, with aggregate metrics, per-task curves, multiple seeds, confidence intervals, sample-efficiency comparisons, wall-clock measurements, and memory-budget comparisons.
The ablation study is useful and supports the importance of the KL regularizer and HL-Gauss critic loss, especially under smaller on-policy batch sizes.
The paper is well motivated and clearly connects pathwise gradients, surrogate critic quality, and trust-region-style policy constraints.
weaknesses: The novelty is mostly an effective synthesis of known components rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic principle; several ingredients are drawn directly from SAC, REPS/MPO-style KL regularization, TD-lambda/GAE, HL-Gauss, layer normalization, and auxiliary self-prediction.

There are several technical/presentation issues in the algorithm specification: the KL multiplier update equation appears to repeat the entropy constraint instead of using the KL constraint, the TD-lambda equations and loss notation are inconsistent, and some pseudocode details do not fully match the surrounding equations.

Reproducibility is weakened by missing or malformed references such as the absent code URL and a placeholder reference to implementation details in “??”; important implementation details are deferred to code that is not actually specified in the manuscript.

The empirical comparison, while strong, is not fully comprehensive: FastTD3 is only compared on a subset, ManiSkill lacks strong off-policy baselines, and some baselines are taken from prior benchmark implementations with different budgets or seed counts.

Theoretical support is limited. The paper motivates why on-policy pathwise gradients should work with an accurate critic, but does not provide formal guarantees or direct quantitative analysis of critic-gradient bias versus score-function variance.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, especially around robustness and generality; the evaluation is restricted to GPU-parallelized continuous-control benchmarks and does not test image observations, real-robot transfer, or non-MPS settings despite discussing broader memory advantages.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and nontrivial problem in continuous-control reinforcement learning: making pathwise policy gradients practical in an on-policy setting, where PPO-style score-function estimators can be high variance and off-policy actor-critic methods require large replay buffers.

The proposed REPPO recipe combines plausible stabilizing components, including maximum-entropy exploration, KL-constrained policy updates, categorical critic regression via HL-Gauss, layer normalization, auxiliary self-prediction, and multi-step/TD(lambda)-style targets.

The empirical section is broader than a minimal benchmark: the paper evaluates on MuJoCo Playground/DMC-style tasks and ManiSkill tasks, reports aggregate and per-environment curves, includes wall-clock comparisons, reliability metrics, ablations, and a memory-budget comparison with FastTD3.
The paper is mostly understandable and includes pseudocode, hyperparameter tables, and implementation discussion, which makes the intended algorithmic structure reasonably clear.
weaknesses: The contribution appears to be primarily an engineering combination of known ingredients rather than a clearly novel algorithmic advance. Pathwise gradients, entropy regularization, KL/relative-entropy constraints, categorical critics, target-style stabilization, layer normalization, and auxiliary prediction all have substantial precedent, and the paper does not convincingly isolate a new core idea.

The central claim that robust on-policy pathwise policy optimization is enabled by REPPO is not technically well supported. The method depends on learned Q-gradients from recent on-policy data, but the paper provides no meaningful convergence analysis, bias analysis, or rigorous argument that the critic gradients are reliable enough for policy improvement.

The empirical comparison is not strong enough for a top-tier venue. PPO is the main on-policy baseline, while comparison to strong modern actor-critic and constrained policy optimization methods is limited. The results leave open whether improvements come from pathwise gradients specifically, from architecture/loss choices, from tuning effort, or from weaker baselines.

Several important baselines and connections are underdeveloped, including MPO/VMPO-style KL-constrained actor-critic methods, SVG-style methods, natural policy-gradient/TRPO variants, SAC-style on-policy ablations, PQN-related continuous-control adaptations, and recent GPU-parallelized RL systems.

The ablations do not fully disentangle the many moving parts. Since REPPO bundles KL regularization, entropy tuning, HL-Gauss, layer normalization, auxiliary prediction, target choices, batch-size choices, and sampling choices, stronger factorial ablations are needed to establish which components are necessary and how they interact.

There are technical and presentation issues that reduce confidence. For example, the entropy/KL tuning equations appear inconsistent in the extracted text, with the KL multiplier update seemingly using the entropy constraint; the main text also contains a broken reference to implementation details as “??” and an unfinished code-availability sentence.

The evaluation metrics and claims are somewhat overinterpreted. Aggregate normalized scores and the proposed “reliable performance” threshold may obscure task-level failures and are sensitive to normalization/threshold choices. Some per-task curves show REPPO is not uniformly superior, but the narrative is more confident than the evidence supports.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Key details are scattered or missing, including exact baseline tuning budgets, environment versions, random seeds for all methods, compute-budget parity, wall-clock protocol, code availability, and exact implementation choices referred to only vaguely as being in the codebase.

The writing has noticeable polish problems, grammatical errors, and imprecise phrasing. These are not fatal by themselves, but combined with the technical ambiguities and incomplete reproducibility they make the submission feel immature for a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: bringing low-variance pathwise policy gradients into a fully on-policy continuous-control setting, with clear motivation around stability, memory footprint, and massively parallel simulation.

REPPO is a coherent algorithmic synthesis: TD-lambda style on-policy Q targets, maximum-entropy exploration, forward-KL policy constraints, adaptive entropy/KL multipliers, categorical value learning, normalization, and auxiliary representation learning fit together well.

The empirical evaluation is strong overall, covering 23 MuJoCo Playground DMC tasks and 8 ManiSkill tasks, with aggregate metrics, confidence intervals, per-environment curves, reliability analysis, wall-clock comparison, and memory-constrained FastTD3 comparisons.

The ablation study is useful and identifies which ingredients are most important, especially KL regularization and HL-Gauss critic learning, while also showing when normalization and auxiliary losses matter.
The paper is well positioned relative to PPO, SAC, FastTD3, MPO/VMPO, Parallel Q-learning/PQN, differentiable-simulation approaches, and recent value-learning stabilization work.
The practical significance is high: achieving PPO-like memory use and wall-clock speed while approaching or matching strong off-policy methods is valuable for GPU-parallelized robotics/RL workflows.
weaknesses: The novelty is partly a careful recombination of known ingredients rather than a single sharply new theoretical idea. The paper would be stronger if it isolated which parts are genuinely essential to enabling on-policy pathwise gradients beyond existing maximum-entropy/KL/value-learning techniques.

The theoretical support is limited. The central claim that the learned on-policy surrogate is accurate enough for reliable pathwise updates is primarily empirical; there is little formal characterization of the bias introduced by the critic gradient or of failure modes under distribution shift from the behavior policy.

The baseline comparison is good but not perfect. Some PPO/SAC results are taken from benchmark authors, seed counts differ across methods, and it is not always clear that all baselines received equally strong tuning under the exact same compute and implementation conditions.

The wall-clock evidence is narrower than the sample-efficiency evidence. It is measured mainly in a JAX setting on L40s hardware, and the appendix notes framework-specific differences; this weakens broad claims about wall-clock superiority.

There are reproducibility and polish issues: the paper contains a missing code URL, a placeholder reference to implementation details as '??', and some apparent equation/pseudocode inconsistencies, such as the KL multiplier update appearing to use the entropy expression rather than the KL expression.

The method still has observed failure cases, such as premature convergence or PPO outperforming REPPO on some tasks, and the paper could do more to diagnose when pathwise updates become biased or exploration becomes insufficient.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: making low-variance pathwise policy-gradient updates viable in a fully on-policy setting, where replay buffers are undesirable or memory-prohibitive.

REPPO is a coherent algorithmic synthesis of on-policy TD-lambda value learning, maximum-entropy exploration, KL-constrained policy updates, categorical value regression, normalization, and auxiliary prediction. The resulting method is practically well motivated and reasonably simple relative to many trust-region or mirror-descent alternatives.

The empirical evaluation is broad for continuous-control RL: 23 MuJoCo Playground DMC tasks and 8 ManiSkill tasks, with aggregate metrics, per-environment curves, sample-efficiency plots, and a reliability metric. The use of many seeds for REPPO/PPO and confidence intervals is a notable strength.
The paper includes useful ablations showing that the KL regularization and HL-Gauss critic loss are important, and that normalization and auxiliary losses matter more under smaller on-policy batches.
The memory-efficiency angle is compelling: comparing REPPO with FastTD3 under large and constrained replay buffers highlights a practical advantage of on-policy pathwise learning.
The exposition is mostly clear, with pseudocode, implementation details, hyperparameters, and an appendix covering discrete-action adaptation and wall-clock caveats.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental. Many ingredients are borrowed from prior work, including entropy regularization, KL-constrained updates, pathwise actor-critic gradients, categorical value losses, normalization, and auxiliary prediction. The contribution is mainly a well-engineered combination rather than a fundamentally new principle.

The theoretical support for using a biased learned on-policy Q surrogate for pathwise gradients is limited. The paper motivates the approach intuitively and empirically, but does not provide much analysis of when the surrogate-induced bias is controlled or how policy improvement is guaranteed under repeated multi-epoch updates.

Some baselines and comparisons are not fully satisfying. SAC and PPO numbers partly come from benchmark papers, FastTD3 uses fewer seeds and different implementation constraints, and wall-clock comparisons exclude several important baselines because of framework issues. This weakens the strongest claims about state-of-the-art efficiency.

The evaluation is strong but still concentrated on GPU-parallelized simulation benchmarks with vector observations. The claims about broad practical utility would be stronger with image-based tasks, real-robot transfer, or domains where memory pressure is truly binding.

The method appears to depend on very large on-policy batches and massive parallelism, e.g. 1024 environments and 50M steps. This may limit applicability outside GPU-simulated robotics/control settings, and the paper could discuss this dependence more directly.

Several presentation and mathematical details need tightening. Some equations and pseudocode contain apparent indexing/sign/notation issues, such as the entropy-augmented reward using the next action in the pseudocode, discount indexing in the TD target, the sign convention for the cross-entropy loss, and the precise KL clipping condition. These are likely fixable but create ambiguity for implementation and review.

The hyperparameter story is positive but not completely clean: some quantities such as discount factor and value support bounds are tuned automatically per environment, and Atari requires a different lambda. The claim of a single robust hyperparameter set should be stated more carefully.
The discrete-action extension is interesting but placed in the appendix and only roughly on par with PQN on Atari-10, so it does not strongly support broad generality beyond continuous control.

strengths: The paper addresses an important RL problem: obtaining lower-variance pathwise policy updates in an on-policy setting without large replay buffers.
weaknesses: The main contribution appears to be an empirical combination of existing ingredients: entropy regularization, KL-constrained updates, TD-lambda targets, categorical value losses, layer normalization, and auxiliary prediction. The paper does not make a sufficiently clear conceptual or theoretical advance beyond this combination.

There are serious clarity and possible technical issues in the algorithm specification. For example, the KL term is written using log pi_old / pi_new while being described as a KL constraint in the opposite direction, and the condition in Eq. 15 is hard to reconcile with the stated constrained objective. The HL-Gauss loss is also written without the usual negative sign. These may be notation errors, but they make the central method difficult to verify.

The evaluation is narrower than the claims suggest. Results are concentrated on GPU-parallelized continuous-control benchmarks, with no real-robot, pixel-based, offline-to-online, or broader control settings. This limits evidence that REPPO is generally robust or practically preferable to established algorithms.

The baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. FastTD3 is excluded from wall-clock comparisons due to framework differences, RPO/DPO are reported as unsuccessfully tuned, and PPO/FastTD3 comparisons may be sensitive to implementation, network size, update budget, and tuning effort.

The method has many interacting components, and while ablations are provided, they mostly show that several borrowed components are necessary. This weakens the claim that pathwise gradients themselves are the key driver rather than implementation scale and stabilization details.

The wall-clock and memory claims are overstated. The paper acknowledges framework-specific timing issues, yet still uses wall-clock efficiency as a major selling point; memory advantages over off-policy methods are plausible but not enough to establish a stronger algorithmic contribution.
The discrete-action extension is not compelling: it performs roughly on par with or slightly below PQN on Atari-10, so it does not substantially broaden the contribution.

Overall, despite some strong empirical results, the paper feels incremental and under-specified in places. I would be concerned about acceptance at a top-tier AI conference without a clearer algorithmic contribution, cleaner formalization, and more rigorous/fair comparisons.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem in reinforcement learning: obtaining the stability and memory advantages of on-policy methods while exploiting lower-variance pathwise policy gradients that usually depend on off-policy replay.

REPPO is a clear and practically meaningful algorithmic contribution, combining on-policy TD-lambda Q learning, entropy regularization, KL-constrained policy updates, and modern critic-stabilization techniques into a coherent method.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall: 23 MuJoCo Playground DMC tasks, 8 ManiSkill tasks, additional Atari-10 discrete-action results, multiple seeds, aggregate metrics with confidence intervals, and per-environment curves.

The paper includes useful ablations showing that KL regularization and HL-Gauss critic learning are especially important, with additional analysis of normalization, auxiliary losses, and data/buffer size.

The comparison considers several relevant baselines, including PPO, SAC, FastTD3, RPO, DPO, and PQN in the discrete setting, and the memory-efficiency comparison against FastTD3 is particularly compelling.

The method appears practically valuable: it improves sample efficiency and reliability over PPO while retaining an on-policy memory footprint, and the claimed availability of both JAX and PyTorch implementations strengthens reproducibility.
The writing is generally clear, with good motivation for why pathwise gradients are attractive but difficult in an on-policy setting.
weaknesses: The novelty is partly compositional: many core ingredients are adapted from prior work, including SAC-style entropy tuning, REPS/TRPO-like KL control, TD-lambda targets, HL-Gauss value learning, layer normalization, and auxiliary representation learning. The paper’s main novelty is the integration and empirical demonstration rather than a fundamentally new theoretical mechanism.

The technical justification for why the learned on-policy Q surrogate yields reliable pathwise gradients remains mostly empirical. Since the policy gradient is biased through an approximate critic, stronger analysis or diagnostics of critic error versus policy improvement would make the central claim more convincing.

Some baseline comparisons are not fully clean. Several results are imported from prior papers or use different implementations/horizons, FastTD3 is run with fewer seeds, and wall-clock comparisons exclude important off-policy baselines because of framework differences.

The method has many interacting components and hyperparameters despite being presented as robust. Although ablations are helpful, the paper could better quantify sensitivity to key settings such as KL target, entropy target, lambda, critic capacity, and HL-Gauss bin ranges across benchmark families.

The evaluation is strong but still concentrated on GPU-parallelized simulator benchmarks. It is less clear how REPPO behaves in slower simulation, real-robot data regimes, image-based observation settings, or environments where on-policy data collection is expensive.

The claimed wall-clock advantage should be interpreted cautiously because implementation framework, JIT compilation, hardware, and network size substantially affect the conclusion, as the authors themselves note.
There are minor clarity and polish issues, including typos, a dangling code-availability sentence in the extracted manuscript, and at least one unresolved reference marker in the HL-Gauss discussion.
